name: Pectin
short: Cases: gut blockage on pectin-mix thickeners (newborn title); citrus pectin anaphylaxis (woman, 2 children); gel tube feed blocked airway (man). With chamomile, 255 children: side effects as placebo.
text: Allergy (case reports): a woman in her twenties with a known nut allergy had anaphylaxis after a sports drink containing citrus-derived pectin; skin tests were positive to the drink, citrus pectin, lemon seed and cashew, and the authors describe a rare but clinically significant cross-allergy between cashew nuts, citrus seeds and citrus pectin contaminated with citrus seed allergens. A 12-year-old girl with cashew allergy had a sore throat after gummies containing citrus-derived pectin and a mild sore throat on a supervised challenge with citrus pectin powder; skin prick and basophil activation tests were positive to citrus/apple pectin powder (as the abstract groups them), although she had no symptoms after apple-derived pectin gummies at home; the authors diagnosed a cashew-associated citrus seed allergy, most likely to citrin, and say that people with suspected pectin allergy should also be closely examined for citrus seed allergy. A 3½-year-old boy with cashew allergy had anaphylaxis after a fruit smoothie containing citrus pectin, with a positive skin prick test to pectin; the authors conclude that eating pectin, not only breathing it in, can cause allergic reactions. A 7-year-old girl with earlier anaphylaxis to cashew nuts had a barking cough and itching about two hours after eating a frozen Citrus unshiu (a mandarin); skin and basophil tests to a commercial pectin product were positive, and on challenge she had abdominal pain and nausea only when the pith (albedo), which is rich in pectin, was eaten with the fruit; the authors attribute the reaction to the pectin, and the record's title calls it anaphylaxis. Further reports are titled 'Anaphylaxis in a pectin- and cashew nut-allergic child caused by a citrus bath' (a bath, not by mouth) and 'Pectin-induced occupational asthma' (breathed in at work); these records have no abstract, so nothing more can be reported. Children with diarrhoea (apple pectin with chamomile, a combination taken by mouth): in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 255 children aged 6 months to 6 years, treatment was well tolerated, with adverse effects similar to placebo; the abstract of an earlier 79-child trial gives no adverse-event data. Tube feeding: in a randomised trial in 201 patients fed by stomach tube for 1 week, a pectin-containing formula that gels in the stomach led to fewer feeding-related events than a standard formula, including diarrhoea in 2 of 98 versus 13 of 100. A case report describes an 82-year-old man given a semi-solid feed through a nose-to-stomach (nasogastric) tube, a feed containing pectin and calcium phosphate that turns from liquid to semi-solid in the stomach; after 14 days he had sudden respiratory failure from tracheal obstruction caused by reflux and aspiration of the feed, and recovered after intubation. The authors say the safety of such feeds by nasogastric tube is not well confirmed and that reflux of semi-solid feeds can be more fatal than reflux of liquid feeds, in their words. Feed thickeners (pectin added to milk): a case report describes intestinal obstruction and enterocolitis, probably caused by inappropriate use of thickened feeds; the abstract does not give the patient's age, the amount used, or what this patient's thickener contained (the record's title names a branded product). The authors say that feed thickeners have an important part in treating reflux in infants, that pectin and silicium have been added to milk to thicken feeds, and that they may form an obstructive bezoar (a solid mass that blocks the gut). Another record, with no abstract, is titled 'Neonatal intestinal obstruction. 2 cases in newborn infants fed pectin and cellulose food thickeners'. The abstracts of two placebo-controlled trials of pectin-based raft-forming anti-reflux tablets (88 and 65 patients) and of a study of pectin liquid added to tube feeds in 18 children with cerebral palsy give no adverse-event data. Interactions: in six healthy volunteers, pectin added to a formula diet taken with digoxin (a heart medicine) did not lower average blood digoxin levels, but the peak level was reached later than without the additive.
